lead: Induction heating passes a high-frequency current through a coil and lets the metal part heat itself. Eddy currents and hysteresis inside the workpiece convert the coupled magnetic energy into heat, so the coil stays cooler than the charge. The method is clean, fast and local: it melts steel in a crucible, softens a billet for forging, hardens a gear surface, and boils a pan on an induction cooktop. Only a few universities teach its design as a full topic. This chapter shows the skin-depth choice, the transformer model and the inverter that drives the coil.
prereq: You need: the full-bridge inverter (DC-AC inverters) and resonant converters with soft switching (DC-DC converters).

sections.h3: Heat is made inside the metal

blocks.text: A work coil carries a high-frequency AC current and creates an alternating magnetic field. The metal to be heated, the workpiece, sits inside this field. The field induces eddy currents in the workpiece; its resistance turns those currents into heat. In magnetic steel, hysteresis also adds heat on every magnetisation cycle. The coil itself stays cooler because its resistance is small and it is water-cooled.
δ is skin depth in m; ρ is workpiece resistivity in Ω·m; f is coil current frequency in Hz; μ is workpiece permeability in H/m, equal to μ<sub>r</sub> μ<sub>0</sub>.

Below the Curie point (about 770 °C) magnetic steel has μ<sub>r</sub> of about 100 and ρ of about 2 × 10⁻⁷ Ω·m, so δ is only 3.2 mm at 50 Hz and 0.23 mm at 10 kHz. Above the Curie point μ<sub>r</sub> falls to 1 and hot steel's ρ rises to about 1.2 × 10⁻⁶ Ω·m, so δ grows to 78 mm at 50 Hz and 5.5 mm at 10 kHz. The hot stage is the hard one, so the frequency is chosen for hot steel. Choose f so δ is smaller than the billet radius; then current crowds near the surface and heats it fast. The coil and workpiece act as a transformer with a shorted single-turn secondary. The workpiece reflects a resistance R<sub>ref</sub> into the coil; P ≈ I<sub>coil</sub>² R<sub>ref</sub>. Magnetising inductance makes the coil current lag, so power factor is low and a capacitor is added.

A resonant inverter converts DC to the coil frequency. In a series load-resonant inverter, the coil and a capacitor form a series resonant tank; the current is near sinusoidal and the inverter switches near zero current. A parallel load-resonant inverter puts the capacitor across the coil and gives a near-sinusoidal coil voltage. The soft-switching ideas are those of resonant DC-DC converters.

Power is set by frequency or DC link. Above resonance the tank is inductive; moving f closer to resonance raises current and power. Changing DC link voltage V<sub>d</sub> changes coil voltage and power. Control must track load changes: cold steel, hot steel, and steel above the Curie point all have different μ and R<sub>ref</sub>. Coupling gap and coil turns also change R<sub>ref</sub>; poor coupling lowers efficiency.

sections.h3: Design steps for a billet or crucible

items: Find metal power: P<sub>metal</sub> = m c ΔT / t. Add melting or latent heat if the charge melts.
Divide by overall efficiency η (often 0.5 to 0.7) to get inverter output P<sub>inv</sub> = P<sub>metal</sub> / η.
Choose f from the skin-depth formula for hot steel: make δ about one-third to one-half of the billet radius, so f = ρ / (π μ δ²). Small parts need 10–100 kHz; large billets use 1–10 kHz.
Choose coil turns N and voltage V<sub>coil</sub>; coil current I<sub>coil</sub> = P<sub>inv</sub> / (V<sub>coil</sub> × pf). Use the actual pf from the resonant tank, not 1.
Water-cool the coil: copper losses I<sub>coil</sub>² R<sub>coil</sub> become heat; keep coolant flow enough to hold coil temperature.
Check coupling, Curie point and duty cycle; tune the tank capacitor at the working frequency.

spec.aria: Chain of DC link, full-bridge inverter, tank capacitor and work coil above a section of a 50 millimetre billet whose top and bottom layers, 12.5 millimetres thick, carry the eddy current.

examples.question: A steel billet of diameter 50 mm and length 100 mm is heated from 20 °C to 900 °C in 60 s. Density 7850 kg/m³, specific heat 500 J/(kg·K), overall efficiency 60 %, coil voltage 400 V at 0.3 power factor. Hot steel has ρ = 1.2 × 10⁻⁶ Ω·m and μ<sub>r</sub> = 1. Find the inverter output power, the coil current, a frequency that gives δ equal to half the radius, and the tank capacitor that brings the inverter to unity power factor.
steps: Metal power P<sub>metal</sub> = E / t = 6.78191 × 10⁵ / 60 = 11,303 W.
Inverter output P<sub>inv</sub> = P<sub>metal</sub> / η = 11,303 / 0.60 = 18,839 W ≈ 18.8 kW.
Coil current I<sub>coil</sub> = P<sub>inv</sub> / (V<sub>coil</sub> × pf) = 18,839 / (400 × 0.30) = 157 A.
Frequency: δ = r/2 = 12.5 mm. f = ρ / (π μ<sub>0</sub> δ²) = 1.2 × 10⁻⁶ / (π × 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 0.0125²) = 1945 Hz; take f = 2 kHz (δ = 12.3 mm).
Capacitor: Q = V² ω C, so C = 59.9 × 10³ / (400² × 2π × 2000) = 29.8 µF, about 30 µF.
With the capacitor supplying the vars, the inverter carries only the real power: I<sub>inv</sub> = 18,839 / 400 = 47.1 A instead of 157 A.
examples.answer: The inverter delivers about 18.8 kW, the coil carries 157 A, a 2 kHz supply gives δ ≈ 12.3 mm in hot steel, and a 30 µF tank capacitor cuts the inverter current to 47 A.

import math
d = 0.050
L = 0.100
rho = 7850.0
c = 500.0
T1 = 20.0
T2 = 900.0
t = 60.0
eta = 0.60
V = 400.0
pf = 0.30
vol = math.pi * d**2 / 4.0 * L
m = rho * vol
E = m * c * (T2 - T1)
Pm = E / t
Pin = Pm / eta
I = Pin / (V * pf)
print(round(vol, 7))
print(round(m, 3))
print(round(E))
print(round(Pm))
print(round(Pin))
print(round(I))

f=1.2e-6/(math.pi*mu0*0.0125**2)
Q=V*I*math.sqrt(1-pf**2)
C=Q/(V**2*2*math.pi*2000)
print(round(f), round(Q), round(C*1e6,1), round(Pin/V,1))

traps: Using the skin depth of cold magnetic steel for the whole cycle. Above the Curie point δ becomes about 25 times larger at the same frequency, so the frequency is chosen for hot steel.
Thinking the coil makes most of the heat; the coil is water-cooled and the heat is in the workpiece.
Forgetting the reflected resistance and low power factor; coil current is not P/V, it is P/(V × pf).
Treating the Curie point as a fixed number; above it μ<sub>r</sub> falls sharply and δ, R<sub>ref</sub> and power all change.
Designing the tank at one load only; cold, hot and molten workpieces change the resonant frequency and coupling.

quiz.q: Write the skin-depth formula for induction heating and define each symbol.
quiz.a: δ = √(ρ / (π f μ)); δ is skin depth in m, ρ is workpiece resistivity in Ω·m, f is frequency in Hz, μ is permeability in H/m.

quiz.q: Why does the heat appear mainly in the workpiece and not in the coil?
quiz.a: The coil has low resistance and is water-cooled. The workpiece is a shorted secondary: induced eddy currents meet its resistance and make I²R heat, and magnetic steel adds hysteresis loss.

quiz.q: A steel has ρ = 2 × 10⁻⁷ Ω·m and μ<sub>r</sub> = 100 at 10 kHz. Find δ.
quiz.a: δ = √(2 × 10⁻⁷ / (π × 10⁴ × 100 × 4π × 10⁻⁷)) ≈ 0.23 mm. The current is confined near the surface.

quiz.q: A 2 kg steel block is heated by 100 K in 30 s. Specific heat is 500 J/(kg·K) and overall efficiency is 0.6. Find the inverter output power.
Why does the coil current and power change when the steel passes the Curie point?
quiz.a: Above the Curie point μ<sub>r</sub> falls to about 1. The coil inductance falls, so the tank's resonant frequency rises; δ grows and R<sub>ref</sub> and hysteresis loss fall. The controller must follow the new resonant frequency (often with a phase-locked loop) and may raise the DC link voltage to hold the power.

quiz.q: Why is the coil power factor low, and how does a capacitor help?
quiz.a: The coil has large magnetising inductance, so current lags voltage. A capacitor supplies the magnetising VARs, raises power factor and reduces the inverter current rating.

quiz.q: Give two industrial uses of induction heating and one domestic use.
quiz.a: Industrial: billet heating before forging, crucible melting or surface hardening. Domestic: induction cooktop.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry design goes further into coupled electromagnetic-thermal finite-element simulation, where coil geometry and water cooling are optimised together. Search for 'induction billet heating', 'skin depth', 'series resonant inverter' and 'Curie point' to go deeper. Newer work uses SiC inverters at higher frequency to shrink the coil and improve efficiency for small parts.
